analysis.one_liner: Requires large electric suppliers to get 6% of their power from renewables in 2013, rising to 25% by 2025.
analysis.headline: The bill had 11 cosponsors but the Senate Energy Committee never acted on it; it got no hearing, no vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a national renewable electricity standard: large electric suppliers would have had to get a growing share of the power they sell from renewable sources like wind, solar, and geothermal, starting at 6% in 2013 and reaching 25% by 2025. Suppliers could meet the target by generating or buying renewable energy credits, or by paying a fee. Money from those fees would have gone to states for renewable energy promotion and for energy assistance and weatherization for low-income households.
analysis.who_benefits: Renewable energy generators, who would get a guaranteed and growing national market for their power plus tradable federal credits; low-income households, who would receive energy assistance and weatherization funded by suppliers' compliance payments; small on-site generators and projects on Indian land, which would earn double or triple credits; and the public broadly through a shift away from fossil generation over two decades.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a graduated requirement for large retail electric suppliers, rising from 6% renewable generation in 2013 to 25% in 2025 and staying there through 2039.
It establishes a federal system for issuing and tracking renewable energy credits and lets suppliers buy, sell, exchange, or borrow credits to comply, creating a national market for renewable energy.

Suppliers that choose to pay instead of comply make alternative compliance payments, and that money goes into a state grant fund for promoting renewable energy and for energy assistance and weatherization services for low-income consumers.
Generators on Indian land earn two credits per kilowatt hour, and small on-site facilities (1 megawatt or less) earn three credits per kilowatt hour, steering investment toward those communities.
The bill explicitly preserves state authority to adopt stronger renewable energy programs than the federal standard and to regulate how credits are acquired and used.

analysis.who_pays: Customers of the large electric suppliers subject to the standard, who would bear the cost of renewable power through their rates; the bill expressly allows rate-regulated utilities to recover the full cost of renewable energy purchased to comply. Suppliers selling under 1 million megawatt-hours a year, rural electric cooperatives, and government-owned utilities are exempt unless they choose to join.
analysis.who_pays_short: Customers of large regulated electric utilities

drawbacks.text: Electric utilities with rate-regulated sales may recover the full prudently incurred incremental cost of renewable energy obtained to comply, so the bill's costs would be passed through to customers rather than absorbed by shareholders.

Suppliers can meet the requirement by paying an alternative compliance payment capped at the lesser of 200% of the market value of credits or 3 cents per kilowatt hour, which in some regions could be cheaper than building new renewable generation and let fossil plants keep running.

The standard excludes rural electric cooperatives and government-owned utilities, and applies only to suppliers that sold at least 1 million megawatt-hours in the prior year, leaving part of the electricity market outside the mandate.

Biomass, including material from public lands under defined conditions, counts toward the requirement, which supporters of stricter forest protections would object to even with the bill's limits on old-growth and roadless areas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have pushed the electricity system toward renewable generation over more than two decades while funding low-income weatherization and energy assistance out of compliance payments. Its design leans on customers, though: utilities can pass compliance costs straight to rates, the 3-cents-per-kilowatt-hour compliance-payment cap gives fossil-heavy suppliers a cheap way out, and co-ops and government utilities are exempt. It is a genuine climate and market-building measure, but a customer could reasonably worry about paying for it first.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never reached the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall of New Mexico introduced the bill on April 6, 2011, joined by 10 Democratic colleagues and one Independent.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where it remained.
No further action — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's complete action history before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-heavy electric utilities that would have faced the mandate are better off, since they never had to buy renewable credits or make compliance payments, and their customers never saw the rate increases that cost recovery would have produced. Renewable developers and the low-income assistance programs the bill would have funded got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil-heavy utilities that avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no recorded roll call exists to measure the split.

industries.industry: Renewable energy generators (wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, incremental hydropower)
industries.note: A federal standard reaching 25% by 2025 would have guaranteed these generators a growing national market, with tradable federal credits to sell. Small on-site projects and projects on Indian land would have earned double or triple credits.

Suppliers falling short would have had to buy renewable credits or pay up to 3 cents per kilowatt hour in alternative compliance payments, and their fossil generation would have lost market share as the requirement rose. The outcome of the bill means they avoided those costs entirely.

The bill would have imposed a compliance obligation on large investor-owned suppliers, but it also guaranteed them recovery of the full prudently incurred cost of renewable energy from their rate-regulated sales, shifting the burden to their customers.

industries.industry: Rural electric cooperatives and government-owned utilities
industries.note: These suppliers were carved out of the standard unless they voluntarily opted in, so they avoided the mandate's costs while the burden fell on the large regulated suppliers' customers. Some co-ops could have benefited from selling credits if they chose to participate.
